tip: Add -la/-le to a noun to build a manner adverb. heyecan (excitement) becomes heyecanla, meaning with excitement.
The yes/no word mu stands as its own word, harmonizes, and carries the person ending: istiyor musun means do you want.
The -ma ending turns a verb into a noun. kapanmak (to close) becomes kapanması, the closing of it, with -sı marking whose.
olarak means as or in the role of and turns a word into an adverb: gönüllü olarak means voluntarily, as a volunteer.
bakmak (to look) needs -e/-a on its object: bisiklete bakıyor means looking at the bicycle, never a plain object form.
To say I want you to do something, use verb+ma plus a possessive and -ı: olmanı istiyorum means I want you to be.
The aorist -r marks habits and routines, not this moment: kalkar means gets up as a rule, matching genellikle (usually).
sevmek takes its object in -i, so walking becomes yürümeyi (yürü+me+yi): yürümeyi seviyorum means I like walking.
Add -ınca to a verb for when or as soon as: çıkınca means once I leave. İşten çıkınca means after leaving work.
The ending -elim/-alım means let's: bin (get on) becomes binelim, meaning let's get on.
Verb + -dığında means when that happens: durduğunda means when it stops. Yağmur durduğunda, when the rain stops.
The -ş in buluşmak makes it reciprocal, done to each other: buluşacağım means I'll meet up with someone, not meet alone.
adjective + bir şekilde builds a manner phrase like English -ly: ciddi bir şekilde means seriously, in a serious way.
az önce means a moment ago and pairs with the simple past: gittin means you went, so the sentence says you just went.
Verb + -erek says by doing, describing how: yürüyerek means by walking, on foot. yürüyerek giderim, I go on foot.
-abil means can or might: olabilir means it can be or may be. tehlikeli olabilir, it could be dangerous.
Pair -den (from) with -e (to) for a route: okuldan eve means from school to home.
önümüzdeki literally means the one in front of us and is how Turkish says next: önümüzdeki yıl means next year.
The -mış past reports something inferred or heard, not witnessed: olmuş and gelmemiş mean he apparently got sick, didn't come.
After a length of time, önce means ago: iki gün önce means two days ago.
Possession links two nouns: the owner takes -ın, the thing takes -si. Komşumuzun kedisi means our neighbor's cat.
To say behind, the thing takes -ın and arka takes -sında: Dağın arkasında means behind the mountain.
Infinitive + için means in order to: cevabı bulmak için means in order to find the answer.
ki opens a wished-for clause whose verb ends in -sın: İstiyorum ki ... olsun means I want it to be, with olsun as let it be.
Turkish drops the verb to be in the present: mandalina çok ucuz is literally mandarin very cheap, meaning mandarins are cheap.
Verb + -ken means while doing: giderken means while going. işe giderken, while going to work.
gibi means like or similar to and follows the noun it compares: arkadaş gibiyiz means we are like friends.
Turkish sees a dream rather than has one: rüya gördüm is literally I saw a dream, the normal way to say I dreamed.
Verb + -meden önce means before doing: gitmeden önce means before going. işe gitmeden önce, before going to work.
arasında means between and follows both nouns joined by ile: Ev ile okul arasında means between the house and the school.
The ending -dir adds a formal, matter-of-fact tone: ailedir means it is a family, stated as a general truth.
Repeating a word builds a step-by-step sense: damlaya damlaya means drop by drop, showing a gradual action.
Put en before an adjective for the most: en sıcak means hottest. en sıcak günü, the hottest day.
Verb + -mişti marks an earlier past, had done: izlemiştim means I had watched it before, prior to now.
ile after a noun means by means of: feribot ile means by ferry. It can also contract to feribotla.
For we need to, use verb+me plus -miz plus gerekiyor: gitmemiz gerekiyor means we need to go.
lazım means needed or necessary and follows the thing required: bilet lazım means a ticket is needed.
Many verbs pair a noun with etmek (to do): tercüme etmek means to translate, so tercüme ediyor is she is translating.
The bare verb stem is the command form for sen: al means take. şemsiyeni al, take your umbrella.
Adding -t makes a verb causative, to make someone do it: gülümsetiyor means makes one smile, from gülümse (smile).
Add -ca/-ce to an adjective to form an adverb: hızlı (fast) becomes hızlıca, meaning quickly.
sayende is a set phrase meaning thanks to you, crediting someone for a good result: Senin sayende, thanks to you.
Insert -ama before the ending for cannot: bırakamıyorum means I can't put it down, from bırak (leave, drop).
daha before an adjective means more, making the comparative: daha iyi means better. The thing compared takes -den.
hem ... hem means both ... and, placed before each item: hem sağlıklı hem eğlenceli means both healthy and fun.
Adding -ıl makes a verb passive: satmak (to sell) becomes satılıyor, are being sold, with no named seller.
Verb + -dıkça means as or the more that happens: geçtikçe means as it passes. Yıllar geçtikçe, as the years go by.
Siz is the polite or plural you and its verb ends in -sunuz: bekliyorsunuz means you wait, matching Siz.
var means there is or, with a possessive, have: planlarım var means I have plans, literally my plans exist.
